How NoteDown keeps notes on several devices in step, how single notes are
shared with other people, and how everything stays end-to-end encrypted —
without accounts: the server knows no email, name or password, only
anonymous identities and the relations created by scanning a code.
Decided with the user on 2026-10-13; built in the app phase. The prototype
carries the merge logic (`app/js/core/merge.js`, tested in
`tests/merge.test.mjs`) and the whole UI with a simulated server.

## Principles

- **Local first.** Every device holds a complete, readable copy of the
  user's notes and works fully offline. The server is a relay and backup
  of encrypted files, never the primary copy.
- **End-to-end encrypted.** The server stores only ciphertext. It never
  sees a note's text, title or status, nor a key that could decrypt one.
- **Plain Markdown stays the format.** Each file is a normal NoteDown file
  (`docs/file-format.md`); encryption wraps the whole file for transport
  and storage on the server.
- **No accounts.** An identity is a key pair; devices and contacts are
  connected by scanning a QR code or opening a link (reason: no email
  service, no login flow, and keys come straight from the other person
  instead of from the server).
- **Standard building blocks only** — no home-made cryptography.

## Files: one per circle of people

- The user's **private file** holds every note that isn't shared.
- Every note shared with the same set of people lives in that set's
  **shared file**: notes shared with A and B in the A+B file, notes shared
  with A, B and C in the A+B+C file. The private file is the set of one.
- A file's member set **never changes**. Sharing a note with one more
  person, or removing one, moves the note into the file of the new set
  (created on first use). So a file's key never has to be rotated.
- Moving leaves a **moved marker** in the old file (`docs/file-format.md`),
  so an edit someone made in the old file at the same time follows the
  note instead of creating a duplicate (see "Merging"). Markers are
  dropped 30 days after the move.
- **All members are equal:** each can edit, close, reopen and delete a
  shared note, share it with further people, remove people, or leave.
  The whole note is shared, including status and due date — closed for
  one means closed for all.
- **Removing someone** stops their access to every later change; what
  their devices already decrypted cannot be taken back.
- Notes are shared with **contacts** only (see "Contacts"); someone who
  doesn't use NoteDown yet gets an invitation link first.
- The main view shows the notes of all files together; which notes are
  shared and with whom is part of the UI round.

## Where the files live

| Platform | Location |
|---|---|
| Android, iOS | The app's documents folder, visible in the system's Files app: `notes.md` plus one file per shared set (named after its members) |
| Web | Browser storage (IndexedDB); download and import as Markdown files |

A user-chosen folder (e.g. an Obsidian vault) can follow later. Devices
rely on the operating system's own storage encryption for the local copy.

## Identity and devices

- **Turning on sync** creates the identity: a random **recovery key**
  (≥ 128 bit, shown once as groups of letters and digits, to print or
  store safely) from which the **identity key** is derived, plus a key
  pair for this device. Until then the app works fully without sync.
- **Every device has its own keys** (X25519 for encryption, Ed25519 for
  signing), created on the device as **non-exportable WebCrypto keys**
  in the app's browser storage (IndexedDB) — in the web app and in the
  Android app's web view alike (decided 2026-10-13: one code path; the
  Android Keystore would need a native plugin and Android 13+). The web
  view needs Ed25519 and X25519 in WebCrypto (current Android System
  WebView). The identity key itself stays on no device; it only signs the
  start of the **device list**, and every later change to that list is
  signed by a device that is on it at that point.
- **The server knows an identity only by an ID, its public keys and its
  device list.** The ID is a hash of the public identity key, so a
  restoring device finds it from the recovery key alone. A device proves who it is by signing a challenge
  with its own device key; there is no login, code or password.
- **Linking a device:** the new device (e.g. the web app on the desktop)
  shows a QR code with its public device keys, a relay slot and its
  suggested name; a linked device (e.g. the phone) scans it, asks for
  confirmation, adds the key to the device list, wraps the file keys for
  it and leaves the identity, sealed for the new device, in the slot
  (format: `docs/server-api.md` → "Linking a device"). The desktop needs
  no camera, and since the key comes from the QR code, the server can't
  slip in its own; a forged slot answer fails, because the new device
  only joins a verified device list that holds it.
- **Removing a device** (lost, stolen, sold) from another one takes it
  off the device list, so the server refuses it, and **renews the keys**:
  the remaining device creates new file keys for every file the removed
  one could read, re-encrypts those files and wraps the new keys only for
  the devices still listed (the files are small; this takes seconds). The
  removed device can't read anything changed afterwards; what it had
  already decrypted can't be taken back. Neither the identity, the
  recovery key nor the contacts change. (Decided over only blocking the
  device, which leaves it able to decrypt later copies, and over a new
  identity, which needs a new recovery key and warns every contact.)
- **Restoring:** the recovery key counts as one more device — file keys
  are always wrapped for it too — so entering it on a new device brings
  everything back, the only way when no linked device is left. All
  devices and the recovery key lost means the server copies can't be
  decrypted any more (the price of end-to-end encryption); members of
  shared files keep those notes.
- **Own name:** the user picks a display name; it only travels inside
  QR codes, links and encrypted files, never in plain text to the server.

## Contacts

- **In person:** a contact shows their QR code ("My code"), the user
  scans it. The scanning device gets the contact's public key directly —
  the contact is verified by construction. The scanned device receives
  a contact request and confirms it, so both have each other.
- **Remote:** the user sends an **invitation link** through any
  messenger. It carries the user's key fingerprint and a one-time token;
  whoever opens it (installing NoteDown or opening the web app first)
  becomes a contact on both sides. As safe as the channel it was sent
  over.
- Contact names are **local**: the user names a contact; the contact's
  own display name is the suggestion.
- The app remembers each contact's key and warns if it ever changes.

## Keys

| Key | What for | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Recovery key | Seed of the identity key and of the recovery "device" key | Only with the user; never sent anywhere |
| Identity key (Ed25519) | Who the user is: contacts remember it; signs the start of the device list | Derived from the recovery key when needed, stored on no device |
| Device keys (X25519, Ed25519), one pair per device | Unwrapping file keys; proving the device to the server; signing device-list changes | Private keys only on that device, non-exportable (WebCrypto, IndexedDB) |
| File key (AES-256-GCM), one per file | Encrypts that file | On the server once per device of every member (and per recovery key), each copy wrapped for that device's public key; renewed when a device is removed |

- **Sharing a note in a new set of people:** the device creates a random
  file key, wraps it for every device on each member's device list,
  including the user's own (X25519 + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM, as in
  HPKE, RFC 9180), encrypts the file with it and uploads both. A device
  list counts only if its chain starts with the identity key the user's
  app remembered for that contact, so the server can't add a device. Members' devices
  pick up their wrapped key with the file on their next sync.
- Files are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, a fresh nonce per upload, which
  also detects any change to the ciphertext. All primitives are in
  WebCrypto in current browsers and in the app's web view.

## Sync

- Each file is synced on its own: **download** it with its version number,
  **upload** it only if the server's version is still the one the device
  started from. If another device was faster, the device downloads,
  merges and uploads again.
- Sync runs **automatically**: shortly after a change, when the app opens
  or comes back to the foreground, when it reconnects, and every 30 s
  while it is visible (the server has no push). While a note is being
  edited, remote changes wait until the edit ends. A status indicator
  shows synced, syncing, offline or an error (e.g. "This device was
  removed from sync").
- **Linking with the recovery key** combines the notes already on the new
  device with the synced ones; an untouched welcome note is dropped, so
  only one remains.
- Each device keeps, per file, the last state it synced (the **base**).
  A device rejects a version older than the one it has seen, so the
  server can't roll a file back unnoticed.

## Merging

`mergeNotesFiles(base, local, remote)` compares both sides per note id
against the base:

| Local vs. base | Remote vs. base | Result |
|---|---|---|
| unchanged | anything | remote |
| changed | unchanged | local |
| changed | changed | merged per field: status (with closed date), due date and text are taken from whichever side changed them; if both changed the same one, the later-modified side wins — except the text, where the other version is kept as a **conflict copy** (a separate note), so nothing is lost |
| changed | deleted | the edit wins, the note stays |
| changed | moved to another file | the edit follows the note into that file, or into the user's private file if the user is no longer a member there (`applyDisplaced`) |

The merged file keeps the remote order and appends notes only the local
side has, so a merge that adds nothing equals the remote file and two
devices don't keep re-uploading the same notes in each other's order.

## Server

- Holds: anonymous identities (ID, public keys, signed device
  list), files (ciphertext + version, file keys wrapped per device) and
  which identities may access which file, and short-lived relay slots
  for linking devices and contacts.
- Sees, unavoidably: which anonymous identities share files, file sizes,
  times of change and IP addresses — no names, emails or contents.
- **Abuse protection** without accounts: a storage quota per identity
  and rate limits per IP address; payment, if it comes, can stay
  anonymous (an account number instead of an email).
- Creating a file for a member set that already has one returns the
  existing file, so two devices sharing at the same time don't split it.
- Built to scale as a stateless API (Python, FastAPI) with Postgres for
  identities and access; for the test phase Postgres holds the encrypted
  files too, an object store follows when size calls for it (`PROJECT.md`
  → "Technology direction"). The protocol byte for byte is
  `docs/server-api.md`; rate limits per IP are not built yet (backlog).

## Open points

- Until a lost device is removed, it can change or delete notes,
  including shared ones; a version history on the server (backlog #7)
  would let the user bring a file back.
- The UI is decided and in the prototype (`docs/requirements.md` → "Sync
  and sharing" → "Where it is operated"). Real sync covers milestone 1
  (`app/js/sync/`); the rest is simulated in the sample.
- **Milestone 1 client details:** the private file is the identity's only
  file on the server (milestone 2 needs a way to tell it from shared
  files); device names live in the private file (`docs/file-format.md` →
  "Device names"), since the server knows none; the notes still sit in
  `localStorage`, only the keys in IndexedDB.
